notes:
I found plenty of verse-by-verse comment on Genesis 23. I found nothing on the denominational sites themselves (ligonier, desiringgod, lcms, 1517, ag.org and others), and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about this chapter. So the "tradition" notes below come from each tradition's classic teachers as reprinted on studylight, biblehub and blueletterbible. I also didn't find any NET Bible translators' notes or Bible Odyssey articles. Ideally the Lutheran and Orthodox gaps would be filled from the denominational sites themselves, which I didn't reach.

**v. 1: Sarah's age**
- She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is given, which shows how highly Scripture regards her. Isaiah 51:1–2 and 1 Peter 3:3–6 hold her up as an example for believing women. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- The Pulpit Commentary works out that Isaac would have been 37. It sees the repeated wording ("these were the years of the life of Sarah") as meant to make Israel remember its ancestress's age. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Adam Clarke (Methodist) says the promise of Christ's coming became explicit with Sarah and was fulfilled with Mary, so God honoured these two women above all others. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-23.html

**v. 2: Death and mourning**
- Abraham grieved deeply, but not like those who have no hope (1 Thessalonians 4:13). His tears were not weak or faithless. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the first Hebrew verb as beating the breast and the second as quieter weeping. "In the land of Canaan" may stress that she died in the promised land. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- *Where Abraham "came" from (old commentators disagree):* As the Pulpit Commentary reports it, Calvin denied that Abraham had been away, while Luther thought he had gone to Gerar. Clarke says he came from Beersheba, about 24 miles off. Others say he simply turned to the work of mourning or went into Sarah's tent. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/genesis-23.html
- John Gill (Baptist) mentions, and rejects, a story that Sarah fainted and died on hearing of Isaac's offering. He thinks Abraham simply went from his own tent to hers. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-2.html
- John Wesley (Methodist) says Abraham did more than perform the customary rites: his grief was sincere, which is why the text uses both "mourn" and "weep." https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/
- Matthew Henry notes that the special friends of heaven still die. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_023.cfm

**v. 3: Rising from beside his dead**
- The Pulpit Commentary pictures Abraham sitting on the ground through the days of mourning, then going to the city gate once his grief had eased (citing Calvin). The Hittites were descended from Heth, son of Canaan. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Matthew Henry says arranging the funeral can help keep grief from overwhelming us at first. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_023.cfm

**v. 4: "A foreigner and an outsider"**
- Abraham felt this way because his true home was heaven (Hebrews 11:9–10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- Clarke, drawing on Hebrews 11 and 1 Peter 2:11, says the words describe the state of Abraham's mind more than of his body. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-4.html
- Barnes: as a "stranger" (not a Hittite) Abraham had no burial ground; as a "sojourner" (a resident, not a passing visitor) he could ask to buy one. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-2.html
- Utley reads the two words together as one idea: a resident alien who owns no land. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-23
- Gill points out that Abraham owned no ground at all. Wesley says the death of loved ones should remind us we are not at home in this world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-4.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary calls this the Bible's first mention of a grave. It sees Abraham's wish to own the plot as faith that the land would belong to his descendants. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html

**v. 6: "God's chosen one" (literally "a prince of God")**
- Calvin (Reformed): Hebrew attaches God's name to whatever excels, so the phrase means a man of rare excellence. He sees "some seed of piety" in the Hittites for honouring God's gifts in Abraham. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-6.html
- Wesley and Matthew Henry: "not only great, but good." Abraham called himself a stranger and they called him a prince, because those who humble themselves are exalted. https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-moses-called-genesis/
- Barnes: a chief clearly favoured by God, as shown in his call, his deliverance in Egypt and his victory over the kings. Some of this the Hittites had seen for themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-6.htm
- The Cambridge Bible suggests the flattering words may hide the Hittites' unwillingness to sell a grave. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-6.htm
- Constable says the Hittites offered the use of a tomb but avoided handing over land, which would have ended Abraham's landless status. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-4.html
- Utley says the Hebrew *elohim* here can simply mean "mighty," describing a powerful local leader. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-23
- The Pulpit Commentary adds that one man speaks for all, and "my lord" just means "sir." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html

**v. 7: Abraham bows**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls the bow a mark of respect that fits Eastern manners. He declined their offer politely but firmly, out of faith, love for Sarah and self-respect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/genesis/23.htm

**vv. 8–9: The request for Machpelah**
- "If you are willing" is literally "if it is with your soul." It shows Abraham respecting local custom and authority. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64465/
- The Pulpit Commentary says go-betweens were expected in such dealings. It notes that "full silver" is the first mention of money in the Bible. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Abraham had lived nearby and built an altar there earlier (Genesis 13:18). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- *Meaning of "Machpelah":*
  - Matthew Poole: "double," either separate caves for men and women or an entrance cave leading to the tomb. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-9.htm
  - Ellicott says "among you" is a mistranslation. Abraham didn't want Sarah buried among the Hittites; he wanted the sale witnessed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-9.htm

**vv. 10–11: Ephron "gives" the field**
- *Was Ephron generous or shrewd?* The split runs across traditions, not along denominational lines.
  - Polite but shrewd: Guzik says the opening "gift" was a custom the seller expected the buyer to refuse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
  - Constable thinks the offer was meant to stop Abraham paying less than the asking price. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-14.html
  - More generous: the Pulpit Commentary doubts these words were empty politeness in that earlier age, and sees offering the whole field as possible goodwill. Ephron sat among the townspeople as a leading citizen, not necessarily a magistrate. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
  - The Holman Bible Dictionary says both men knew a sale would follow. https://www.studylight.org/dictionaries/eng/hbd/m/machpelah.html

**vv. 12–13: Abraham insists on paying**
- The Pulpit Commentary takes Abraham's pleading tone to mean he thought the offer was at least partly sincere. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Abraham refused the gift out of fairness and good sense, not pride. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-4.htm
- Clarke: being religious gives no one the right to be rude. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/

**vv. 14–15: Four hundred shekels**
- *Fair price or overpriced?*
  - High: Coffman calls it exorbitant, comparing Jeremiah's 17 shekels for a field. Constable compares David's 50 shekels for the temple site. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-15.html
  - Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) calls it "the sucker's price" and says Abraham, in his grief, didn't haggle. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-15.html
  - JFB: Ephron's offhandedness was "mere affectation." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-15.html
  - Generous: Wesley and Henry read Ephron as caring little for money and preferring to oblige a friend. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Gen/Gen_023.cfm
  - Ellicott calls it "no mean price." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-15.htm

**v. 16: Weighed out**
- Shekels were weights of silver, not coins. "The standard of the merchants" meant weight accepted in trade. The Canaanites were among the earliest traders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-15.htm
- Guzik: Abraham's dealings show how believers should do business: courteously, fairly and prudently. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- Matthew Henry: honest dealing can stand the light. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/genesis/23-15.htm

**vv. 17–18: The deed**
- The text stresses that the land was Abraham's by legal deed as well as by God's promise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- Listing the trees matches later deeds. The public sale at the gate meant many witnesses. "Deeded" is literally "stood up," meaning confirmed. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Utley: with this, Abraham owned land and was no longer a landless alien. https://bible.org/seriespage/genesis-23

**v. 19: The burial**
- Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah were later buried here, which made it the Tomb of the Patriarchs. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/genesis-23/
- Rachel is the only one missing. The burial rites are unknown. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- A sermon quoted on Precept Austin argues the chapter's main point is that Sarah was buried "in Canaan," showing faith in the future. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64465/
- Another links it to Abraham's belief that God raises the dead (Hebrews 11:17–19). https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64465/

**v. 20: A burial site in the promised land**
- The cave is a "down payment" on the promise; a permanent family tomb showed confidence that death was not the end. https://biblehub.com/genesis/23.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary calls a grave the only thing a man can really own. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- *The Acts 7:16 puzzle:* Stephen says Abraham bought a tomb at Shechem. Proposed answers include:
  - Stephen merged two purchases into one.
  - A copyist added "Abraham" (Calvin, Beza).
  - Abraham bought two plots.
  - A mistake by Stephen or Luke.
  The Pulpit Commentary finds none of these fully satisfying. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/genesis-23.html
- Chuck Smith takes the two-purchase view. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/genesis/23-19.html

**Other views**
- *Catholic:* The Catholic Encyclopedia says the Hebrew always writes "*the* Machpelah," naming the place where the field is. The Greek, the Targum, the Syriac and the Vulgate render it "the double cave." https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09502a.htm
- Jerome accepted a rabbinic tradition, built on a misreading, that Adam was buried here as a fourth patriarch, and put it into the Vulgate. The encyclopedia accepts the Haram in Hebron as the real site. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/09502a.htm
- The Crusaders made it the church of Saint Abraham. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07184a.htm
- *Reference works on netbible.org:* the dictionary entries (Easton, ISBE) say there is no doubt about the site. They describe it as east of Mamre and revered by Christians, Jews and Muslims. https://classic.net.bible.org/dictionary.php?word=Machpelah
